newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EMU debate seen intensifying between Bonn and Paris.
newsitem.headline: EMU debate seen intensifying between Bonn and Paris.

text.p: The confidence expressed in Amsterdam this week over Europe's planned single currency will probably fade quickly given underlying tension between Germany and France over key aspects of monetary union.
In a sense, analysts say the rift between the two powers, papered over on Monday in often obscure and indecipherable EU-speak, has a certain air of inevitability.
As the euro's 1999 launch date draws near, Germany and France are being forced to take a much harder look at the deal hammered out in the Dutch town of Maastricht five years ago.

Moreover, with preparations and expectations for the euro's introduction accelerating after each EU summit and ministerial gathering, the opportunities for countries to influence the shape and form of the final product are becoming ever fewer.
"The journey that lies ahead is not easy," said Sweden's Prime Minister Goran Persson.
Among the issues under reexamination two seem to stand out.
The first concerns the Maastricht Treaty's entry criteria, in particular the requirement that governments bring their 1997 budget deficits down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product.
French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Tuesday underlined France's more liberal approach to the target in clear and precise language.
"I think, as we have always said, the most important thing is to be approaching three percent, what we call trending towards three percent," Strauss-Kahn told French radio.

Analysts say it is no secret that France's budget outlook is likely to look more dire after an audit of the government's finances later this month. There has been speculation that the deficit ratio could climb as high as 3.8 percent of GDP.

The trouble this poses for Prime Minister Lionel Jospin is twofold -- he has committed himself to meeting the euro's 1999 deadline but on terms that are more amenable to the French public -- in other words, less budget austerity.

Meanwhile, Germany, having been long-wedded to a strict interpretation of the deficit target, now finds itself in an embarrassing and uncomfortable position given the problems it too is having in getting expenditure under control.
The fiscal distress might require a more generous reading of the criteria by Bonn's European partners if Germany is to enter EMU on schedule.

It also makes it tougher for Bonn to argue for the kind of budgetary rigour believed necessary for the euro to have a lasting credibility. Finally, the greater room there is for fiscal slackness the larger the potential number of initial members -- another thorn in Germany's side.

"The problems of the German and French budgets -- particularly for 1998, will now come into focus and these are likely to prove much more politically intractable," said a report by analysts at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.
Another contentious issue is the future exchange rate policy orientations of the European Central Bank (ECB)

One of the additions to the conclusions of Monday's political resolution on jobs was an invitation to EU ministers and the European Commission to study the ways in which the euro's value is managed against the dollar or other non-EMU currencies.
Importantly, the language stressed that the way in which the euro's policy is implemented should be "without prejudice to the primary objective of (the ECB) to maintain price stability."
Bonn and Paris have already agreed to the creation of a Stability Council, an informal grouping of EU finance ministers and central bankers to discuss economic policy in the euro area.

But many analysts say there are limits on how far France can influence the ECB's policy. If there is one area of the Maastricht treaty that is unambiguous it is the independence given to the central bank.
"France is going to win the battle on the budget front but Germany will win on monetary policy," said Bruce Kasman, European economist at J.P. Morgan in London.
